items.description: Στα 13, η Jeeva Subramanian έφτασε στο Chennai με 300 Rs που της είχε δώσει η μητέρα της. Ο αδερφός της την είχε συνοδεύσει στην πόλη, αλλά την άφησε στη στάση του λεωφορείου του Koyambedu. Μη γνώριμη με το μέρος και χωρίς πού αλλού να πάει, τον περίμενε να επιστρέψει. "Δεν ήξερα κανέναν στο Τσενάι. Νόμιζα ότι ο αδερφός μου θα επέστρεφε να με πάρει, οπότε συνέχισα να περιμένω…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 13, Jeeva Subramanian arrived in Chennai with Rs 300 her mother had given her. Her brother had accompanied her to the city, but left her at Koyambedu bus stand. Unfamiliar with the place and with nowhere else to go, she waited for him to return. "I did not know anyone in Chennai. I thought my brother would come back to take me, so I kept waiting in the same place. I would go to the public toilet, wash myself and my clothes, and return to where I had been sitting. I kept thinking he would look for me there," she recalls. Two days passed before Jeeva realised that he was not coming back. By then, she had spent nearly three days at the bus stand. A woman who worked there cleaning the premises eventually approached her and offered to find her a job. That conversation led to Jeeva's first job in Chennai, at a shop inside the bus stand. She earned Rs 40 a day, with food and accommodation provided by the employer, though her wages were held back for seven days at a time. At 13, Jeeva waited two days at Koyambedu before accepting her brother would not return. Photograph: (Instagram/ @jeeva_subramaniam.offl ) "I was only 13. That was my first job in Chennai . They gave us food and a place to stay, so I continued working," she says. The job lasted about two months. When it ended, the bus stand became her refuge again. She slept within sight of a police booth because she felt safer there, and took up whatever work she could find, including carrying vegetables at the Koyambedu market in the early hours of the morning. At the time, Jeeva knew she was a girl, but did not know what it meant to be transgender or that there was a community of people like her. "I lived with the feeling that I was a girl. I did not know there was a transgender community. I was a child. I did not understand what was happening around me," she says. From surviving to finding her place Jeeva eventually found work clearing used banana leaves after wedding functions at a marriage hall. But workers were asked to leave once a wedding was over, and she was again left searching for somewhere safe to stay. A visitor at one of the functions gave her a contact for a housekeeping company. Through it, she found work at a sweets outlet in Vadapalani, earning Rs 2,200 a month, along with food and accommodation. Around this period, Jeeva began to understand her identity and gradually encountered other transgender people. Dance offered another possibility . She joined a dance school and began performing at programmes, sometimes wearing wigs for devotional and glamour songs. When the programmes stopped, she was once again left looking for work. A friend helped her find occasional performances, but that too came to an end when he moved to Dubai. On Dharma Durai's set, Vijay Sethupathi's warm embrace gave Jeeva the courage to continue acting. Her next opening came through cinema, where she began working as a touch-up assistant. She had already developed an interest in acting, but expressing that ambition was not easy. People questioned whether she was good-looking enough to act, and once they learnt she was transgender, some became reluctant to employ her. "I used to tell people that I wanted to act, but they would ask me, 'What are you going to do by acting? Are you beautiful enough?' They would dismiss the idea. After they found out that I was trans, people became hesitant to take me for work. Some of the other assistants would keep teasing me," she says. There were, however, people who stood up for her. Actor Bala Singh, with whom she worked for several years, was particularly protective. Jeeva remembers him telling others, "She is my daughter. Why are you talking about her like that?" She also worked with actors including Anushka Shetty, Taapsee Pannu, Shriya, and Ramya Nambesan. Actor Shriya encouraged her to learn makeup, a skill that could support her financially. Jeeva went on to work as a bridal makeup artist , doing makeup for around 400 brides. But discrimination followed her into this profession too, and a bad experience eventually forced her to give it up. Jeeva created Dorothy's look herself, gaining 13 kilograms and sending photographs to convince the filmmakers. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) Even as she found ways to earn, the search for a stable home remained unresolved. The rooms she could afford were often in poor condition, with rainwater entering the house and collecting up to her knees. The 2015 Chennai floods damaged her home and left her with very little. A friend, Sheela, took her in and gave her food and shelter. These experiences had already taught Jeeva how precarious everyday life could be. But it was on a film set that she encountered a moment of acceptance that would change how she saw her place in the industry. The embrace that changed her relationship with cinema By the time she was called to work on Dharma Durai , Jeeva was considering leaving Chennai. She had worked for years, tried different jobs and felt that none of it was taking her anywhere. She accepted the opportunity partly because she admired actor Radhika. The shoot, however, was difficult. People in the crowd used slurs against her, and she found it hard to continue performing. She broke down and cried. Actor Vijay Sethupathi noticed what was happening, intervened, and asked the crowd to stop. He told them, "She is my younger sister," before hugging Jeeva and kissing her forehead. For someone who had experienced rejection and abuse, the gesture carried a meaning that went far beyond the film set. "An embrace may be a normal thing for other people, but it did not come to me so easily. I cannot even put into words what I felt that day. When he hugged me, I closed my eyes for a moment, and it felt as though the whole universe was spinning around me. Nobody had hugged me like that before. He kissed me on the forehead, and I held on to him and cried," she says. Her short film won 58 awards, yet recognition did not guarantee steady work or housing. Director Seenu Ramasamy then encouraged her to continue with the scene, telling her that the very people insulting her should one day whistle and applaud when they saw her on screen. "He could have said that they should get someone else to do the scene. Instead, he told me to act with confidence. That gave me the courage to go back and perform. That is the magic of Dharma Durai for me," she says. The film was released in 2016, and Jeeva began to be recognised by people who had seen her on screen. Her father, too, called her "my daughter", a moment she remembers with particular happiness. But the recognition did not translate into a steady livelihood. People who had earlier hired her as an assistant began to see her only as an actor and stopped calling her for makeup work. "I had to start running around for work all over again. Earlier, at least I was working as an assistant. After the film, people would say, 'You have become an actor. How can we call you for assistant work?' Nobody called me. I struggled ten times more than I had before. There were days when I could not find food. I would go to the Vadapalani temple and eat the food they distributed. I even went to Hyderabad and stayed in a small lodge, calling actors and asking them to take me on as a makeup assistant so I could pay my rent," she says. After neighbours objected, a landlord returned the ₹40,000 advance Jeeva had paid for a house. Photograph: (Deccan Chronicle) Being visible on screen, she realised, did not necessarily mean being accepted off it. Jeeva continued looking for work, taking up roles in films and short films. One of her short films went on to win 58 awards, while her work brought her opportunities in projects including Airaa , Darbar and Suzhal . But she did not want recognition to be mistaken for charity. She wanted opportunities to demonstrate her ability, and that determination would be tested again when she auditioned for Dorothy . Proving what she could do in Dorothy When the team behind Dorothy approached Jeeva, they initially felt she looked too young for the character. They were looking for someone older and heavier. Jeeva, who weighed around 64 kg, decided to gain weight and shape the character's appearance herself. She gained 13 kg, choosing a cotton saree, double nose studs, a bun and grey hair to complete the look. She took photographs of herself and sent them to the team. "I told them, 'Give me one opportunity. Only if you give me a chance can I prove myself.' I wanted them to see that I could do the character. I put together the look, took the photographs myself and sent them. I was determined to get this opportunity," she says. Jeeva also performed the physically demanding sequences herself, without a body double. During one sequence, she was hurt, and actor Karthi helped her up and checked on her. When the crew applauded her performance, he came over and hugged her. "He came running and hugged me tightly. He even helped me because I had been hurt. I felt that same kind of embrace I had received years ago during Dharma Durai ," she says. Jeeva's Diwali cake marked celebration after years of spending the festival alone behind closed doors. Photograph: (Still from Dorothy) The film became another turning point. At a rough-cut screening, Jeeva was moved by what she saw and hugged director Karthik Subbaraj. He told her they would take the film to Canada. At the Toronto International Film Festival in 2026, she experienced a warm welcome from people who had watched her work. Actor Rajinikanth also praised her performance. Yet, even as her work travelled beyond India and more people began recognising her, the difficulties she faced away from the camera did not disappear. In fact, being more recognisable sometimes made finding a house even harder. The struggle to find a home continues Jeeva has been searching for a house for around six months. A property that would ordinarily be rented for Rs 10,000 has been quoted to her at Rs 30,000. She once paid an advance of Rs 40,000 for a house, only for the landlord to return the money after neighbours objected to a transgender woman moving into their street. The questions she faces from brokers and landlords are often invasive. They ask how many people will visit her, whether she intends to bring clients home, and how many people she will bring in each day. In one instance, a broker suggested that she would have to pay far beyond the advertised rent. Jeeva has also been told that a house could be rented to her only if a male acquaintance signed the agreement, because the landlord did not trust her on her own. "I have been looking for a house for six months. If a house normally costs Rs 10,000, they tell me it will cost Rs 30,000. I paid Rs 40,000 as an advance for one house, and then the people in that street said that a transgender person should not be allowed to live there. They told the owner to return my advance. This is what keeps happening," she says. Beyond international applause for Dorothy, Jeeva hopes for a 400-square-foot home where she can rest. She recalls being asked questions that implied she was offering sexual services. When she explained that she went to work and could pay only what she earned, she was told not to pretend to be poor. A transgender woman who approached the same broker was quoted Rs 35,000 and managed to secure a house, Jeeva says, making her feel that access to housing can depend on how much a landlord believes a person can pay. The uncertainty has affected her daily life. Her belongings have been packed and unpacked repeatedly as brokers promise that a house will be confirmed the next day. She has kept much of her household packed for months and says she has cried after conversations with people who were supposed to help her find a place. Jeeva has also approached the government for assistance. She says she was once told that a house could be allotted to her, but the property was around 50 km away, making it impractical for her work. When she sought an allocation closer to the city, she was told that housing categories had specific allocations for several communities but no separate percentage for transgender applicants. She is now trying to secure an appointment with the minister to submit a formal request. Jeeva wants neither charity nor special treatment; she wants affordable housing and dignity without interrogation. "I do not want anyone to give me a house for free. If I have to pay Rs 4 lakh or Rs 5 lakh, I am willing to do that. Just allot me a small house. I have faced so many things in life, but I have cried more over this house problem than over many of the other things that happened to me. Every time I go to look at a house, the questions people ask me are so humiliating. I do not even know how to answer them," she says. She has a simple request: "I want a small house of around 400 square feet, a house that is mine. I do not want to keep proving to people that I am a good person, that I am respectable, or explaining where I am going and what work I do. I just want to sleep peacefully in my own house." The contrast is difficult to ignore. Jeeva has appeared on screens watched by audiences across countries, received appreciation from some of Tamil cinema's most prominent names and represented a community that rarely gets such visibility. Yet she is still made to answer questions about whether she can be trusted with a rental home. A celebration, and a wish for ordinary life The difference between being seen and being allowed to live freely is something Jeeva has experienced in smaller, everyday ways too. She recalls that, in earlier years, Diwali was not a festival she celebrated with others. She would buy enough rice and lentils to last a few days, shut the doors and keep to herself. After Dorothy , she decided to mark the festival differently. She bought a cake and cut it for Diwali. Jeeva's journey is a testament to finding her voice, claiming her place and rewriting what representation can look like. "It may seem like a small thing, but it gave me so much happiness," she says. For Jeeva, the cake was not simply a festive purchase. It was a moment in which she allowed herself to celebrate, rather than spend the day withdrawing from the world. It was also a reminder that the life she wants is not defined only by film roles, awards or public recognition. It includes the ordinary freedoms that many people take for granted: a secure place to return to, the ability to celebrate without fear and the dignity of not having to explain herself to strangers. She continues to look for work and a home, while hoping that the attention around Dorothy will lead to more opportunities. She would like to win a National Award one day. But when she speaks about what she wants beyond cinema, her wish is strikingly modest. After years of being pushed out of homes, workplaces and public spaces, Jeeva is asking for a place where she can close the door at the end of the day and rest without having to prove that she belongs there. The applause may follow her from one theatre to another, but what she is still waiting for is a home of her own.

items.title: Ο ιδιοκτήτης ξοδεύει χιλιάδες σε εορταστική έκθεση παμπ DIY για να ευθυμήσει τους ντόπιους
items.titleOriginal: Landlord Spends Thousands on Festive DIY Pub Display to Cheer Up Locals
items.description: Το πνεύμα των Χριστουγέννων είναι ζωντανό μέσα σε έναν ιδιοκτήτη που ξόδεψε πάνω από 6.500 $ για να δημιουργήσει μια εορταστική έκθεση στο μπροστινό μέρος της παμπ του - όλα για να φτιάξει τη διάθεση των ντόπιων της πόλης του. Ο Christian Ogley είπε στο SWNS ότι η φετινή χρονιά ήταν ιδιαίτερα δύσκολη για τους κατοίκους του χωριού Knaresborough της Αγγλίας με κουτιά σοκολάτας, λόγω του αυξανόμενου κόστους ζωής. Έτσι μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The Christmas spirit is alive and well within one landlord who spent upward of $6,500 on creating a festive display on the front of his pub — all to cheer up his town’s locals. Christian Ogley told SWNS this year has been particularly tough for residents in the chocolate-box village of Knaresborough, England, due to the rising cost of living. So in an attempt to spread some holiday cheer, the 34-year-old purchased the necessary materials and equipment and recruited the help of seven staff members and regulars to put up some twinkling decor on the facade of the pub, Blind Jack’s. SWNS They spent a week building and installing the design, which includes a 16-foot-tall tree as its centerpiece, surrounded by red ribbons and white lights imitating falling snow. “It has been a turbulent year for everyone in the area and across the U.K. to say the least, so I just wanted to do something nice to make people smile,” Ogley said. “So far it has seemed to have done that — we have had many compliments.” Ogley purchased Blind Jack’s in 2017 alongside his wife, Alice Ogley, and the Christmas display isn’t its first claim to fame: Last year, it was crowned the Best Beer Pub in the U.K. at the Great British Pub Awards. He was inspired to make it a bit more festive after visiting New York City and Ireland over the past two years and seeing the effort landlords put into their displays. He decided that he would do the same at his watering hole, something he said isn’t as common in the U.K. “To start with it was just a bit of fun, but as I have been installing it so many people have been wanting to talk to me about it and have been posting it on social media,” the proud landlord noted. “It has given them something positive to talk about and see.” Ogley put on a smaller display in 2025 but decided to go bigger this year — he started designing this year’s project in January by sketching out initial ideas on the back of beer mats. The dad of two studied graphic design at university, which he said “helped him bring” his ideas to life. “Hopefully it can become a bit of a tradition and something locals can look forward to,” he shared. Altogether, the Christmas display has over 10,000 lights and costs around $3.25 a day to run from 12 a.m. to 12 p.m. The operating costs are lower than Ogley expected, which “is great,” he said, “as it means I can keep them on for longer.” SWNS He continued: “The lights mean so much to me and the community, I’m trying to keep them glowing for as long as I can each day.” The spectacle has made it difficult to get work done at times — “so many people want to chat and take pictures in front,” he said — but there is still one finishing touch left: He plans to install two seven-foot nutcrackers. This article was originally written by Charlie Fenton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.description: Εάν έχετε βρει ποτέ τον εαυτό σας να αναρωτιέται αν μια συζήτηση έχει διαρκέσει αρκετά, υπάρχει μια αξιοπρεπής πιθανότητα το άτομο με το οποίο μιλάτε να αναρωτιέται το ίδιο πράγμα. Το πρόβλημα είναι ότι κανείς από τους δύο δεν μπορεί να το καταλάβει. Μια μελέτη του 2021 διαπίστωσε ότι οι άνθρωποι συχνά δυσκολεύονται να τερματίσουν τις συνομιλίες τη στιγμή που πραγματικά θέλουν να τελειώσουν. Και αυτό δεν είναι μόνο…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you’ve ever found yourself wondering whether a conversation has gone on long enough, there’s a decent chance the person you’re talking to is wondering the same thing. The problem is, neither of you may realize it. A 2021 study found that people often struggle to end conversations at the moment they actually want them to end. And this isn’t just a problem between strangers. It can happen even when we’re talking to people we know well. Researchers Adam Mastroianni, Daniel Gilbert, Gus Cooney, and Timothy Wilson conducted two studies of a total of 932 conversations to investigate what happens when people want conversations to end. Even people we know can miss the signal Friends chatting over coffee and smiling. Canva In the first study, 806 people reported on a recent conversation with a friend, family member, or romantic partner. The researchers asked when they had wanted the conversation to end and when they thought the other person had wanted it to end. Often, the conversation didn’t end when either partner wanted it to. It was also common for partners to think the other person wanted to keep talking longer than they did. So the researchers designed a second study that let them see what was happening from both sides. Strangers offered striking results Strangers talking in a cafe. Canva For the second experiment, researchers brought 252 strangers into a lab and paired them up. Each pair was told to talk about whatever they wanted for as little or as much time as they liked, as long as the conversation lasted more than one minute and less than 45 minutes. In similar fashion to the first study, each person privately reported when they had wanted the conversation to end and when they thought their partner had wanted it to end. Only 1.59% of conversations ended at a point when both people wanted them to end . In 46.83% of conversations, both people had wanted the conversation to end earlier than it actually did. The strangers also weren’t very good at figuring out what the other person wanted. On average, their estimates of when their partners wanted to stop were off by more than nine minutes. Basically, two people could be standing there thinking, I wonder when this is going to end , while both were waiting for the other person to make the first move. The researchers described this as a coordination problem . If you want to leave but think the other person wants to keep talking, announcing that you’re ready to go can feel awkward or rude. So you wait. Unfortunately, the other person might be doing exactly the same thing. Sometimes the nicest exit is a clear one Woman waving goodbye. Canva We tend to assume that other people will give us a clear signal when they’re ready to stop talking. The research suggests that’s a shaky assumption. People aren’t necessarily revealing their preferred stopping point, and they’re not necessarily very good at detecting ours. The good news is that means you don’t have to wait for the perfect opening…since it likely will never come. And while the study didn’t test ways of getting out of conversations, experts on the subject have plenty of advice for the moment when you realize you’re ready to go. Psychologist Andy Molinsky recommends giving a reason for ending the conversation. It gives the other person some context instead of leaving them wondering whether you’ve suddenly decided you don’t like them. That doesn’t have to be elaborate. “I need to get going, but it was really nice talking with you” is enough. At a party, etiquette experts at Debretts suggest giving yourself a task that naturally moves you out of the conversation, such as getting a drink or going to talk to someone else. You can also bring another person into the conversation, introduce the two people, and then make your exit once they’ve started talking. Another option is to give the conversation a little runway before you leave. Relationship coach Rachel Greenwald suggests asking one final question before leaving, then ending with a sincere compliment. The idea draws on the “recency effect,” which suggests that the way an interaction ends can influence how positively we remember it. And perhaps the most useful lesson from the study is that you don’t necessarily need to wait for the other person to give you permission to leave. After all, they may be waiting for you, too. The post Two people had a conversation. Researchers asked each when they secretly wanted it to end. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Berlin is putting AI cameras on its streets. An artist made a brilliant shirt to outsmart it.
items.description: Σε φωτογραφίες και βίντεο που τραβήχτηκαν ο Simon Weckert έξω από το σταθμό του μετρό Kottbusser Tor του Βερολίνου, ένα πρόγραμμα υπολογιστή σχεδιάζει ένα πράσινο κουτί γύρω από κάθε πεζό και τον χαρακτηρίζει «άτομο». Ο Weckert, που στέκεται ανάμεσά τους, δεν παίρνει καθόλου κουτί. Η διαφορά είναι το πουκάμισό του, ένα φαρδύ, κοντομάνικο κουμπί που καλύπτεται από θαμπές, κορεσμένες σταγόνες χρώματος. Το ονομάζει Digital…
items.descriptionOriginal: In photos and video Simon Weckert shot outside Berlin’s Kottbusser Tor subway station, a computer program draws a green box around each pedestrian and labels it “person.” Weckert, standing among them, gets no box at all. The difference is his shirt , a loose, short-sleeve button-down covered in blurry, saturated blobs of color. He calls it Digital Camouflage. Weckert is the Berlin artist who went viral in 2020 for pulling 99 smartphones through the city in a wagon, which made Google Maps show traffic jams on nearly empty streets. His new target is the AI surveillance Berlin police have brought to Kottbusser Tor, a busy transit hub in the Kreuzberg district. Police began installing about 30 cameras there in late August. According to the Berliner Kurier , it’s the first time Berlin has put a public space outside its transit system under permanent video surveillance. Software watches the live feeds and alerts officers when it spots behavior it’s built to flag, mainly fights and other emergencies, the German news agency dpa reported . Weckert’s concern is who else gets flagged because systems like this can pick out someone lying on the ground, he told 404 Media , and “homeless people could be detected and police get triggered.” The shirt exploits how detectors learn. They’re trained on millions of example images, so what they actually recognize is a statistical pattern, not a human being. “A ‘person,’ for the machine, is a bundle of visual statistics,” Weckert told Dezeen. He built the print against YOLO , a free and widely used object-detection program. Software generated candidate patterns, he ran each one past the detector, and he kept adjusting until it lost confidence that it was looking at a person. The saturated colors and overlapping shapes are meant to drown out the cues the detector relies on and break up the outline of the body. When 404 Media’s Jason Koebler tried it, the box around him disappeared as soon as he held the shirt in front of himself and came back when he pulled it away. View this post on Instagram Weckert doesn’t claim it beats every system, and his project description says it isn’t a tool for evading police or a guarantee of anonymity. Patterns like this are tuned against one model, usually one specific version of it, and it isn’t known whether the shirt fools the software at Kottbusser Tor, netzpolitik.org reported . It also doesn’t hide anyone’s face. The Kottbusser Tor system doesn’t use facial recognition, according to dpa, but officers who get an alert see the actual footage. The idea has been around for years, and Weckert points to published research . In 2019, researchers at Northeastern University, IBM and MIT printed a pattern on a T-shirt that kept an object detector from spotting the wearer more than half the time in real-world tests. The shirts sell for about $88 on his website, and a share of the proceeds goes to groups defending digital civil rights. The Kottbusser Tor cameras went live in early November for a four-week trial. The Left and Green parties have challenged the police law behind them in Berlin’s constitutional court, and Berlin’s interior senator, Iris Spranger, wants to bring the system to Alexanderplatz, Warschauer Brücke and Görlitzer Park next. The post Berlin is putting AI cameras on its streets. An artist made a brilliant shirt to outsmart it. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: If you’ve ever ordered an almond milk latte, odds are you weren’t picturing yourself participating in a culinary tradition that goes back to the Middle Ages . But almond milk isn’t a modern invention created for the age of newly discovered dietary restrictions and lactose aversion. People in medieval Europe were making and cooking with it centuries ago, and they had a particularly practical reason for doing so. Not to mention a religiously motivated one. When dairy was off the menu, almonds came to the rescue During Christian fasting periods , particularly Lent, medieval rules prohibited the consumption of certain animal products, including dairy, for a good chunk of the year. For cooks accustomed to making rich dishes with milk, butter, and eggs, that created a culinary conundrum. A medieval stained glass panel from Canterbury Cathedral, c. 1175 – c. 1180, depicting the Parable of the Sower, a biblical narrative. Wikipedia Thankfully, almond milk, which had already been well established in Middle Eastern cuisine , offered a solution . For one, it was f airly simple to make . Grind almonds, mix them with water, and strain the resulting liquid. Done. And, once made, almond milk could do milk’s job of thickening sauces, soups, stews, and desserts. Obviously, this chameleonic quality could provide the perfect culinary loophole. A 14th-century German cookbook called Das Buch von guter Speise , for example, features several Lenten fasting recipes that utilize chicken or fish cooked in thick almond milk as a dairy substitute. Other medieval recipes used almond milk with rice, dates, and sugar to make sweet dishes appropriate for Lent. However, if you think almond milk is expensive now… There was one catch, though. Almonds weren’t exactly cheap in medieval northern Europe. They were imported on a large scale , and the cost of getting them there made them a relatively luxurious ingredient. But for cooks who could get their hands on almonds (namely those who worked in wealthy households), they offered a remarkably useful way to keep making rich, satisfying dishes during a fast. Point being, your almond milk latte has a surprisingly old ancestor. It just happened to be invented long before anyone had to ask whether the barista could make it extra foamy. Your oat milk has ancient relatives, too Various vegan milk ingredients. Canva And almond milk was hardly the only plant-based milk with an ancient backstory . Humans have been turning plants into milk-like drinks for thousands of years. Coconut milk, for example, has roots going back roughly 5,000 years, while rice milk was being made in China by around 1000 B.C. Soy milk also has a long history, with references to it appearing in Chinese sources nearly 2,000 years ago. Even oat milk, which can feel like the ultimate symbol of the modern coffee-shop era, has been around for decades. Swedish food scientist Rickard Öste developed the modern version in the 1990s as an alternative for people who couldn’t digest cow’s milk. So while the cartons lining today’s grocery store shelves may be relatively new, the basic idea behind them is anything but. Προτιμώ απερίφραστα να είμαι μόνος μου, κρυφακούοντας ηδονοβλεψικά άλλα πε…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Just one?” This is a question I get asked often, and I’m happy to answer with variations of yes. “That’s right. You got it. One indeed!” It has never bothered me, and on the contrary, it fills me with a tiny sense of self-actualized pride. Dinners, movies , concerts. I unequivocally prefer to be on my own, voyeuristically eavesdropping on other people’s lives. To be clear, I like other people’s company in spurts and love, for lack of a better word, “collecting” people as I move through life. But solitude , for the most part, fits best. This is especially true when it comes to traveling. Swiping that train card, with no one watching my clock, fills me with pure glee. But on a recent trip to my favorite city, London, I hit a bit of a snag. High tea at The Kensington, Photo byCecily Knobler Just one? After joyously getting lost in two red-and-gold-swathed parks, I decided it was time for high tea. So I returned to The Kensington Hotel (where I was staying) and made a reservation for that day at 4:00 p.m. “Just you, Ms. Knobler?” the kind man with the top hat asked at the desk. “If that changes,” I said with a wink, “I’ll let you know.” Clad in a black cashmere sweater and a pink and black checkered miniskirt, I checked in with the hosts right on time. They showed me around the various delicate rooms, so that I could pick my spot. Would it be the library, surrounded by leather-bound books by Dickens? Near a fireplace lightly decorated with silver Christmas tinsel? I settled on a seat by a bay window, as the last drops of the sun were squeezed into the space. But I started to notice, as so many families and friends were seated near me, that it seemed this high tea ritual was meant for two or more. And I began to get a little self-conscious. Was I dressed formally enough? Why did it seem I had cat hair on my sweater (and yet don’t have cat?) What exactly IS Christmas pudding? (Luckily, I didn’t have to answer the final question.) Duchess Anna of Bedford For a little context, the late afternoon tea didn’t become popular until the mid-1800s. In a piece about it for Historic UK , Ben Johnson writes, “afternoon tea was introduced in England by Anna, the seventh Duchess of Bedford, in the year 1840. The Duchess would become hungry around four o’clock in the afternoon.” She simply got too hungry to wait for dinner. Johnson continued, “The evening meal in her household was served fashionably late at eight o’clock, thus leaving a long period of time between lunch and dinner. The Duchess asked that a tray of tea, bread and butter (some time earlier, the Earl of Sandwich had had the idea of putting a filling between two slices of bread) and cake be brought to her room during the late afternoon. This became a habit of hers and she began inviting friends to join her.” The last sentence is key. Friends would join her. Johnson further explains, “This pause for tea became a fashionable social event. During the 1880s upper-class and society women would change into long gowns, gloves and hats for their afternoon tea, which was usually served in the drawing room between four and five o’clock.” Christmas tree at The Kensington Hotel, Photo by Cecily Knobler And yet here I was in my version of long gown just being served alone. And as each presentation was given, from the choice of tea to champagne to finger sandwiches, I had this realization that moments are so fleeting. As each item is served and devoured, we must have immediate gratitude because in an instant…it’s gone! Being with just my thoughts (and these exquisite éclairs) sort of forced an introspection I’m not sure I’d have had otherwise. More than enough But gratitude and presence aren’t exactly novel ideas, though they stood out during the ritual. What especially struck me is how powerful it felt to actually enjoy my own company. After all, Duchess Anna had originally begun the tradition as a solo act. Neither she nor I needed a companion to experience every bit of deliciousness life so often has to offer. That high tea with “only” me was more than enough. View this post on Instagram There will, most likely, always be another cucumber sandwich, another date, another teapot. But having the ability to reclaim a ritual and make it my own was truly one of the most special moments of the trip. I’d do it a thousand more times, if I could. (That said, I did chime into a conversation at the table next to me at one point, when I heard them disparaging the Dallas Cowboys.) On my way out, the man in the top hat asked how everything was. “Just right,” I said. “And for the record, it didn’t change. And it was just perfection.” The post High tea is meant to be shared. Doing it alone in London taught me a profound life lesson. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Mr. Feeny, the iconic teacher and principal at the heart of Boy Meets World , was brought to life and made unforgettable by the acting talents of William Daniels. However, it almost didn’t happen. Daniels famously quit the show after the very first table read of the pilot script. He had too much respect for “the underpaid, underappreciated teachers of this country to portray one of them a fool,” per Daniels’ own biography . He didn’t want to play a goofball educator who was only there for laughs. Luckily, the role was rewritten, Daniels returned to the cast , and the rest is history. But of all the heartfelt, emotional, and wise moments Daniels’ brought us as Feeny, one is permanently etched into the hearts of anyone who grew up watching the show. Mr. Feeny’s iconic farewell The series finale of Boy Meets World , “Brave New World: Part 2”, aired in 2000; well over 20 years ago now. But many Millennials can still remember watching the show’s final scene as if it were yesterday. Mr. Feeny gathers in the classroom with his students Cory, Topanga, Shawn, and Eric one final time. As the seventh season of the show comes to a close, each of the main protagonists is preparing to finally leave the nest. They’ll all be moving away from Philadelphia for the first time, finally leaving Feeny behind. He leaves them with parting words of advice: “Believe in yourselves. Dream. Try. Do good.” Topanga, ever the A-plus student, asks if he means “Do well.” “No, I mean ‘do good’,” he responds. Tearful goodbyes ensue, and the kids go on their way out into the big world. Why Mr. Feeny delivered his final words to an empty classroom The series doesn’t end when Topanga, Cory, Shawn, and Eric file out of Feeny’s classroom for the last time. Standing alone once they’re gone, Feeny delivers perhaps his most famous line: “I love you all. Class dismissed.” It’s a full-circle moment for the Feeny character, to finally admit that even though he was hard on the core students, even though he always kept their relationship professional and fair, yes, he did love them in a unique way and not just the way he loves all of his students. Admitting it to an empty room only added to the payoff. And it also allowed the audience to feel like Feeny, the protective mentor we all wish we’d had, was saying goodbye and “I love you,” directly to us. It’s an incredibly moving and poignant end to a show that meant so much to so many. The emotion inside the scene is what makes it so memorable, and much of it was incredibly real. William Daniels recalls being close to tears while filming his final moment. To this day, Feeny is remembered as one of the best portrayals of a teacher ever to grace the screen; and perhaps one of the most beloved sitcom characters of all time. To kids who grew up watching the show, Feeny’s tough love and wisdom was very real. His final line was the catharsis we all needed as the show came to its inevitable end. Η Vivienne αποδείχθηκε ότι ήταν αλλεργική στο καλαμπόκι, μαζί με τα αυγά, τους ξηρούς καρπούς και τις μπανάνες. Woodard, τότε στέλεχος πωλήσεων στην Coca-Cola, imme…
items.descriptionOriginal: A new Girl Scout cookie , on sale in January, started with a snack that sent a baby to the emergency room . The baby was Denise Woodard’s daughter, Vivienne, and the snack had just two ingredients, peanuts and corn. Vivienne turned out to be allergic to corn, along with eggs, tree nuts and bananas. Woodard, then a sales executive at Coca-Cola, immediately pictured her daughter growing up as the “allergy kid” with the “allergy snacks,” she told Snack Food & Wholesale Bakery magazine. The allergy-friendly options in stores didn’t impress her, so she started baking her own cookies, free of the most common allergens. View this post on Instagram She launched Partake in 2016, selling cookies store by store out of her car, and eventually left Coca-Cola to run it. Keeping it afloat took her 401(k) and then her engagement ring. At least 86 investors turned her down, Woodard told CBS News in 2022. “I took it pretty personal,” she said. View this post on Instagram The first yes came in 2019 from Marcy Venture Partners, the fund Jay-Z co-founded, which led a $1 million round. According to Partake , that made Woodard the first Black woman to publicly raise $1 million for a packaged food startup. That same year, when Partake had exactly one other employee, Woodard told her they were going to make a Girl Scout cookie one day. “I think she thought I had lost the plot!” Woodard told TODAY . Rihanna and H.E.R. later invested, and Partake’s cookies are now sold in thousands of stores. In September, the Girl Scouts announced Girl Scout Sparkables, their first allergy-friendly cookie, developed with Partake. Sparkables are crunchy oatmeal cookies with chocolate chips and colorful sprinkles. They’re vegan and gluten-free, and they’re made in a facility that keeps out the nine major food allergens: peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish and sesame. They go on sale Jan. 12, when Girl Scout Cookie season opens nationally, or sooner in areas where the local season starts earlier. They’re sold only online, for direct shipping, so they won’t turn up at cookie booths. As with other Girl Scout Cookies, the proceeds go to local councils and troops. One of the Girl Scouts selling them will be Vivienne, now in sixth grade. In a Q&A marking Partake’s 10th anniversary this summer, she said, “It makes me happy to know that other kids can feel included like me.” The post Mom started baking Girl Scouts cookies her allergic daughter could eat. Now she’s raised $30 million. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Ezra Frech recovered beautifully after prosthetic leg fell off during emotional final ‘DWTS’ performance
items.description: Αυτή η σεζόν του Dancing With the Stars παρουσίασε μερικές απίστευτες παραστάσεις. Από την Τζούλια Στάιλς που αναδημιουργούσε την εμβληματική της χορογραφία Save the Last Dance μέχρι τον τρυφερό της αφιέρωμα στον ηθοποιό Χιθ Λέτζερ στο 10 Things I Hate About You, υπήρξαν ατελείωτες συναισθηματικές στιγμές. Και ο χθεσινοβραδινός τελικός του DWTS σέρβιρε μια από τις πιο αξέχαστες παραστάσεις…
items.descriptionOriginal: This season of Dancing With the Stars has served up some incredible performances. From Julia Stiles recreating her iconic Save the Last Dance choreography to her tender tribute to actor Heath Ledger in 10 Things I Hate About You , there were endless emotional moments. And last night’s DWTS finale served up one of the most memorable performances in the show’s history, according to viewers. Finalist Ezra Frech and his pro partner, Daniella Karagach, performed an incredible freestyle routine to Linkin Park’s “Numb”. Midway through, Frech’s prosthetic leg accidentally came off during a pivotal moment in the routine. And the way he was able to recover left many viewers in happy tears. Frech loses his prosthetic mid-dance The duo’s performance was during the show’s finale, so the pressure was on. Frech started the routine solo and without his prosthetic, dressed in an all-black silky set that moved with him in a series of emotive modern-style movements. Karagach then appeared on the stage, as Frech had just moments to put his prosthetic on to finish the routine together. But as he began to move and jump down stairs on the stage, it was clear his prosthetic was not secure—and fell off. Like a total professional, Frech continued on with the choreography on just one leg. And he pulled off an incredible feat of strength, lifting Karagach with incredible balance. As backup dancers ripped off Frech’s black set to reveal an all-white one to match Karagach, she was able to grab his prosthetic and hand it to him—which he was quickly able to put on. The two paused for a moment and gave each other a knowing nod and smile as they finished out the routine. View this post on Instagram Frech explains what happened The performance earned a standing ovation from the crowd and judges, who awarded them a perfect score. “Ezra, you are a hero,” Judge Derek Hough said . “This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show.” In an interview following the performance, Frech told Extra more about what was going through his head during the routine—and the moment he lost his leg. “I knew it wasn’t on right,” Frech said. “I haven’t watched the video back, but you can see I’m fidgeting with it as I was running up because it wasn’t on right. Sometimes it will lock into place, even if it’s not on right, so I had to just go. And then when I jumped, I was like, ‘Oh my God, it’s going to come off.’ And then it came off, [and] everything happened so fast. I was prepared to dance the rest of the freestyle on one leg if I had to.” When he lost his leg, Karagach added that she yelled to him, “And I was like, ‘Put on your leg!'” Somehow, Frech was able to hear her. “She yelled, ‘Put on your leg!’ And I heard that immediately. I don’t even know what happened. I blacked out. I don’t know what happened. We did a lift on it? I need to watch it back.” On Good Morning America , Frech shared more about the crazy moment. “Last night was crazy. We started our freestyle without the prosthetic. That was a creative choice,” he said. “And things went a little off script and I wasn’t able to suction my leg on and I knew it wasn’t on. And sometimes, when that happens, it’ll re-suction, but it didn’t. It came off. She told me to put it on mid-dance. I kind of blacked out, and then we ended up finishing the dance.” View this post on Instagram Viewers react On social media , viewers were moved to tears and sang their praises to Frech and Karagach for their resilient and graceful performance: “I need to take tomorrow off so I can recover by watching this over and over again till I’ve cried every last tear.” “The audible gasp we all let out when it happened followed by the tears of the rest of the performance Chills!!!” “going down in history of dwts freestyles ” “can’t stop thinking about how incredible this performance was ” “So inspiring ” “The world is changed after witnessing this dance. A masterpiece.” “Losing his prosthetic made the dance that much more impactful. THAT’S OUR MIRRORBALL CHAMP ” “The head nod and look that they give each other after he puts the prosthetic back on ” “It’s crazy how Dani didn’t even know his prosthetic was off until she saw it on the floor…AFTER he lifted her!” The post Ezra Frech recovered beautifully after prosthetic leg fell off during emotional final ‘DWTS’ performance appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το «Men Without Hats» αποκαλύπτει επιτέλους τι ήταν το «The Safety Dance» και γιατί τους έφερε σε μπελάδες
items.titleOriginal: ‘Men Without Hats’ finally reveal what ‘The Safety Dance’ was and why it got them in trouble
items.description: Αν μεγάλωσες αγαπώντας τη μουσική της δεκαετίας του 1980, πιθανότατα έχεις μερικά εκλεκτικά τραγούδια που δεν μπορείς να βγάλεις από το μυαλό σου. Μερικά κομμάτια γίνονται επιτυχίες επειδή οι μελωδίες τους είναι τόσο πιασάρικες που δεν μπορείς παρά να τραγουδήσεις. Άλλοι γίνονται ύμνοι που καθορίζουν τον πολιτισμό. Το "The Safety Dance" από το συγκρότημα Men Without Hats είναι λίγο και από τα δύο. Το ρεφρέν μάλλον μόλις ξαναπαίχτηκε μέσα σου…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you grew up loving 1980s music , you probably have a few eclectic songs you can’t get out of your head. Some tracks become hits because their melodies are so catchy that you can’t help but sing along. Others become culture-defining anthems. “The Safety Dance” by the band Men Without Hats is a bit of both. The chorus probably just replayed in your head after reading the title. But what exactly is the backstory behind this New Wave banger? Does “The Safety Dance” involve wearing protective goggles? Is it a protest song? Or perhaps a metaphor for safe sex? Luckily for us, Men Without Hats founder and frontman Ivan Doroschuk is finally spilling the tea on social media. He recently shared candid stories about the song’s punk roots and why “The Safety Dance” stirred up so much drama. Punk roots and rebellious dance floors Before becoming a shiny synth-pop staple, Men Without Hats started with gritty punk energy in 1977. Doroschuk formed the group at McGill University in Canada with his brothers Stefan and Colin. Depending on when interviewers asked Doroschuk, the origin of the band’s name seems to differ. In one interview, he describes it as a cheeky pushback against the image-obsessed rock stars of the era that prioritized style over substance. In another, Ivan notes that the name stems from taking a stance against established norms by refusing to wear the standard societal uniform (or hat) that most of us inevitably wear. And in yet another, he claimed that the name sprang from his and his brothers’ refusal to wear hats while growing up in the brutal Montreal winters. By the time their album, Rhythm of Youth , was released in 1982, their sound had morphed towards the electronic. Think Devo out of Ohio and The Human League and Gary Numan from the UK. Men Without Hats’ first single, “The Safety Dance,” captures their personal desire for freedom of self-expression, eventually earning the #3 spot on the Billboard Hot 100. It was written as a direct response to club bouncers in the disco era cracking down on slam dancing, moshing, and Doroschuk’s favorite punk dance move: pogoing. Doroschuk was frequently kicked out of clubs for pogoing (AKA jumping straight up and down) to Blondie’s “Heart of Glass” and the B-52s’ “Rock Lobster.” He noted , “I was kind of mad that they wouldn’t let me dance if I wanted to, so I took matters in my own hands and wrote an anthem for it.” The staying power of this pop culture ballad didn’t stop there. The group leaned into their weirdness by releasing a medieval-themed music video featuring Doroschuk as a Pied Piper-like hero urging people to follow their own path. It became an instant MTV favorite and turned a quirky track into a worldwide smash with a universal message. Wild trivia, Glee gripes, and a Commodore 64 Doroschuk’s recent social media posts feel like hanging out with a walking 1980s music encyclopedia. Fans love hearing him address urban legends, including whether former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s mother sang backup on the hit. The answer is no. But separating the band’s real history from its fun folklore keeps longtime listeners hooked. He also has strong thoughts on how later shows handled their signature song. When Glee covered “The Safety Dance,” Doroschuk was happy the show introduced a whole new generation to the band. However, the Glee cover repeats a common mistake. At one point, the female backup vocalist shouts “danser” (that’s French for dance), which people often mishear as “and sing.” But now you know better. Doroschuk also shares how Men Without Hats pushed the edges of technology in their day. Before sleek modern laptops existed, the band relied on a Commodore 64 computer . Using early home computing tech to run sequences and synth parts live on stage took nerve and ingenuity. If a cable came loose or a program glitched mid-set, there was no safety net. Or Safety Dance, for that matter. Why this 80s classic still makes us smile Hearing Ivan Doroschuk reflect on the song reminds us how joyful and scrappy early synth-pop really was. It came from a defiant DIY spirit that wasn’t afraid to make bold art with whatever gear they could find. That mix of rebellion paired with an infectious pop melody is rare. It explains why “The Safety Dance” still fills dance floors in an instant. People hear that opening beat and feel like they have the permission they didn’t even know they’d been waiting for to go out there and leave their inhibitions behind. The post ‘Men Without Hats’ finally reveal what ‘The Safety Dance’ was and why it got them in trouble appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: What's a birthday party without balloons? For Bengaluru-based entrepreneur and mother of two, Sowmya Jagannath, this was a question she found herself thinking about while planning her daughter's birthday. She wanted to try something different, but would her daughter feel that something was missing? Her daughter loves animals, so Sowmya chose colourful fabric decorations in green and earthy shades. Fabric bunting hung across the room, bringing the animal-themed party to life. There were no balloons to inflate or plastic streamers to pull down after the guests left. Instead, the decorations could be packed away and used again at another celebration. The children had fun, and all of Sowmya's initial worries turned out to be unnecessary. Neither her daughter nor the other children missed the balloons. The decorations came from Matter Party, a Bengaluru-based startup that rents out reusable party d cor made from post-consumer textile waste. Founded by Bhavna Kanoria in March 2025, it offers themed fabric decorations that families can rent, return and pass on for another celebration, instead of buying new items that may be discarded after a single use. For Bhavna, the idea began at home, when her own daughter asked for a planet-themed birthday party. The two made buntings from an old sari , finding a way to make the occasion special with fabric they already had. What began with making planet-themed bunting from an old sari for her daughter's birthday eventually inspired Bhavna to start Matter Party in Bengaluru. That small experiment stayed with Bhavna. It would eventually become a business built around a simple question: could celebrations be beautiful, convenient and less wasteful at the same time? How an old sari sparked a business idea Bhavna has a master's degree in English literature, studied interior design and previously worked as a designer. She had also explored ways of making gifting more thoughtful through earlier ventures, including a gift registry service called Giftistree and Scift, a social gifting platform that allowed people to donate to a cause instead of giving physical presents. The idea for Matter Party, however, took time to develop. After making the fabric bunting with her daughter, Bhavna left it on the back burner for a few years. Towards the end of 2024, she returned to it, thinking about how the same principle could work on a larger scale. Matter Party launched in March 2025. Her first rental was for a Lohri celebration rather than a birthday party. The booking came through a friend of a friend, giving her an early opportunity to see how the idea might work beyond her own home. The business now sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala, a Bengaluru-based waste management organisation with a textile recovery facility. Bhavna buys discarded fabric by weight, with material sorted by colour, and sends it to a tailoring unit to be stitched into decorations. "I work on the designs and handle much of the finishing myself, including attaching cords by hand. The leftover scraps are returned to the recovery facility," she says. The result is a collection of reusable decorations in around 35 themes, from unicorns and dinosaurs to Superman, Harry Potter, rainbows and rustic-chic themes. Families can mix and match colours to suit their party. Matter Party sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala and transforms the discarded fabric into colourful party decorations. Lightweight and fitted with cords at both ends, the pieces can be tied to existing fixtures without complicated installation. Once a party is over, the kit is collected and prepared for its next outing. Bhavna irons the fabric, spot-cleans it with soap and water, replaces cords where needed and checks the decorations before they are rented out again. The aim is to keep the materials in use for as long as possible. For these decorations to make their way into more homes, Bhavna knew she had to make renting them as easy as possible for busy parents. What makes parents choose reusable decorations? When Bhavna began offering reusable party d cor, she realised that leading with sustainability did not always persuade people to try it. "People may not choose it just because it is sustainable," she explains. For many parents, the first questions are more practical: Will the decorations look good? Will they suit the theme? Will they be easy to put up? Will renting them be worth the cost? Each decoration is designed to be used across multiple celebrations, allowing families to rent, return and reuse party d cor instead of buying new ones. That understanding has influenced how she presents Matter Party. She wants families to choose the decorations for their designs, range of choices and convenience, without feeling that they have to compromise on how their child's birthday party looks. The reduced pricing is another part of making the service accessible. The startup currently offers two rental options: a Mini Kit for Rs 1,750, which includes 8-10 buntings and fringes, suited to home parties and smaller venues, and a Party Kit for Rs 3,500, with 16-20 buntings and fringes for larger spaces such as clubhouses and gardens. Both kits also include door or backdrop nets, wreaths and a 'Happy Birthday' banner. A refundable security deposit is charged separately. Customers can book through WhatsApp, choose a kit and arrange for delivery before their event. The decorations are collected after the celebration, so families do not have to find storage space for items they may use only once a year. Bhavna has also tried to make the process of putting up and taking down the decorations simple. The kits arrive ready to use, with cords that can be tied to existing fixtures, and customers can pack them back into the provided bag after the party. Optional party helpers are also available through a service partner for families who need additional support. Sowmya found that the rental model made financial sense, too. When she compared the cost with what she had spent buying decorations separately, she realised how quickly individual purchases could add up. "I had done a calculation of the cost of the balloons and the buntings and all the other stuff that I had bought the previous year, and this was actually cheaper than that. We don't realise because we buy it in parts. One balloon package, one streamer package, then this and that. By the time you add it all up, it actually comes up to the same thing, if not more," she says. From dinosaurs and unicorns to rainbows and Harry Potter, Bhavna's reusable fabric decorations are available in around 35 themes for families to choose from. For Bhavna, this is the kind of shift that could help reusable d cor reach more families: it needs to meet their everyday needs as well as help them reduce waste. 'The children don't miss the balloons' Sowmya has used Matter Party for celebrations built around her children's changing interests. Along with her daughter's animal-themed party, her son has had a Harry Potter-inspired celebration in red and black, and the family has also tried a cricket theme. "The themes will be there, but colours are always the easiest thing to put together in terms of adding that vibe to the party. I love that she has so many different colour options," she says. The designs have also drawn attention from other parents. At her daughter's birthday in September, guests could not stop admiring the d cor. Those conversations have given Sowmya a chance to talk about the idea with other families. An earlier conversation with Bhavna about balloons and the impact they can have on animals had encouraged Sowmya to try celebrating without them. "I was almost scared because I was like, 'Oh my God, if I don't have balloons at the party, how will I manage? Will my daughter be okay?'" she recalls. But the children were happy without them. "Nobody missed the balloon completely. Sometimes you have to take these steps to experience yourself; a balloon is not everything for a party," she says. Shwetha, another Bengaluru-based mother of two girls aged 13 and nine, came to Matter Party for a similar mix of thoughtful design and a more sustainable approach. After every celebration, Bhavna irons and spot-cleans the fabric decorations, replaces cords where needed and prepares the kits for their next rental. "I would try and reuse as much as possible, but having said that, options were limited. So I was very pleased that Bhavna came out with a solution which was a little more comprehensive," she says. Shweta has since used the kits for her daughters' birthdays, including garden and rainbow themes. She likes the range of choices and the convenience of having the d cor delivered and collected. A small placard explaining that the decorations are sustainable also gives guests a way to understand the idea. "Keeping sustainability aside, the design is impeccable. She's thought of various options that you would want to host a party. It's definitely something that people should go for even keeping sustainability outside of it," Shweta says. For Bhavna, feedback like this reinforces the importance of making reusable d cor attractive and practical in its own right. Over 100 kg of fabric gets a second life Since its launch, Matter Party has upcycled more than 100 kg of post-consumer textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. For now, the startup operates only in Bengaluru. Bhavna is mindful of the emissions involved in transporting the kits over long distances and does not want expansion to undermine the purpose of the business. She is also exploring collaborations with party venues, caf s, restaurants and other vendors, along with workshops in schools that could help children understand how celebrations can generate less waste. The business has grown through repeat customers and word of mouth, but Bhavna knows that making sustainable choices commonplace will take more than one rental service. It also means helping families see that they do not have to give up the excitement or personal touches that make a birthday special. That change can extend beyond the decorations. Sowmya, for instance, has given plants as return gifts at her daughter's birthday and has chosen plantable pencils and stationery on another occasion. Bengaluru mother Sowmya Jagannath chose Matter Party's reusable fabric decorations for her daughter's animal-themed birthday, celebrating without balloons. Shweta says using the kits has made her think about what else she might change when planning an event. Bhavna has noticed a similar openness among children in her own family. Her niece and nephew, aged three and six, have started telling their friends to avoid waste. For her, it is a reminder that children can adapt to different ways of celebrating, particularly when those choices are part of the experience from the beginning. Helping families celebrate with less waste Bhavna hopes to grow Matter Party without losing sight of what made her start it: the possibility of making a familiar part of family life less wasteful, without making it less joyful. She does not expect parents to change every habit at once. Choosing reusable decorations, skipping balloons or rethinking return gifts can be a starting point. "The aim is to make these options feel normal rather than like an extra effort reserved for particularly environmentally conscious families," she adds. Since launching in March 2025, Matter Party has upcycled over 100 kg of textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. That is also why she wants to expand through local partnerships instead of simply shipping kits across the country. For her, the way the business operates matters as much as the product it offers. A birthday party may last only a few hours, but the decorations can be part of many more celebrations. For Bhavna, that is the possibility she wants more parents to discover: the colourful bunting that made one child's birthday special could bring just as much joy to another child, without either family having to buy everything new. All images courtesy of Bhavna Kanoria and Sowmya Jagannath

items.descriptionOriginal: When the Delhi house where artist Sumakshi Singh spent her childhood summers was demolished, she found an extraordinary way to bring it back. Using delicate white threads, she recreated its doors, windows, stairs and even its gates. Thousands of kilometres away in Venice, Italy, her childhood home became part of an exhibition that drew around 4.5 lakh visitors. Alongside her work stood a towering bamboo structure inspired by Indian construction sites, a miniature Ladakhi settlement made from discarded egg trays and paper, and sculptures inspired by India's natural landscapes. On 25 November 2026, these creations earned India the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's biggest international art exhibitions. The award was decided by public vote. The winning exhibition brought together installations made from thread, bamboo, cotton, paper and earth, each telling a different story of India. Photograph: (Instagram/@pibindia) Behind the winning exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home , are five Indian artists who took inspiration from everyday materials, childhood memories and generations-old traditions to explore something we can all relate to: what it means to call a place home. Here are the five artists and the fascinating stories behind their creations. 1. Sumakshi Singh: A house recreated in thread Artwork: Permanent Address Imagine walking into a house that is no longer there. That is the experience Sumakshi Singh creates with Permanent Address , an intricate, life-size reconstruction of her family home in Delhi. The artist has recreated the house using embroidered thread and water-soluble fabric. Artist Sumakshi Singh recreated her childhood home in Delhi using delicate white threads, preserving memories of a house that no longer exists. Photograph: (Instagram/@ abirpothi ) The house was built in 1951 by Singh's grandparents, who came to India during Partition. It became the venue for family weddings, reunions and childhood sleepovers. It was also where she spent afternoons learning to knit and embroider with her grandmother. Years later, when the house was demolished, the same craft helped her recreate the place she had always called home. 2. Asim Waqif: Bamboo that tells a story of changing cities Artwork: Chaal Using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, artist and architect Asim Waqif built a 30-foot-high structure in Venice without using a single nut or bolt. The bamboo pieces are bent and tied together, forming a structure that resembles the scaffolding that supports buildings across Indian cities. Made using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, Asim Waqif's installation highlights traditional building materials and craftsmanship. Photograph: (Instagram/ @indiainvenice ) The choice of material is central to the artwork. Bamboo has long been used in traditional construction, but modern building practices increasingly favour materials such as steel and aluminium. Waqif's installation draws attention to this shift and the risk of losing traditional skills, such as bending and tying bamboo to build scaffolding. 3. Ranjani Shettar: A garden suspended in the air Artwork: Under the Same Sky In contrast to Waqif's towering structure, Ranjani Shettar's installation feels like stepping into a floating garden. Inspired by flowers and natural growth, Under the Same Sky features sculptural forms suspended from the ceiling. Shettar created the flower-like sculptures using handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer. Ranjani Shettar's Under the Same Sky transforms handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer into flower-like sculptures suspended in the air. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Working from her studio near Sagara in Karnataka, Shettar has used these materials for nearly two decades. Her installation allows visitors to experience the garden from within. 4. Skarma Sonam Tashi: Bringing Ladakh's homes to Venice Artwork: Echoes of Home What does a traditional Ladakhi settlement look like when recreated thousands of kilometres away? Artist Skarma Sonam Tashi offers an answer through Echoes of Home , an installation inspired by the architecture and landscape of Ladakh. Using papier-m ch , cardboard, egg trays and old paper, he creates a miniature settlement that evokes the region's traditional homes, built using earth, stone and timber. Inspired by Ladakh's traditional architecture, Skarma Sonam Tashi's Echoes of Home recreates a miniature settlement using discarded egg trays, cardboard, papier-m ch and old paper. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Growing up in Ladakh, Tashi was familiar with traditional homes built using locally available earth, stone and timber. Designed for the region's harsh climate, these houses help keep families warm during winter and cool during summer. As concrete and steel buildings increasingly replace traditional homes, his artwork draws attention to generations of knowledge that Ladakh risks losing. 5. Alwar Balasubramaniam: When nature becomes the artist Artworks: Drift and Not Just for Us Sometimes, the most compelling artwork is made from something as familiar as the ground beneath our feet. For these works, artist Alwar Balasubramaniam, also known as Bala, uses clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu to create sculptural panels. The surfaces are marked by natural cracks and fissures, capturing the effects of time and environmental forces. Rather than smoothing over these imperfections, the artist makes them the focus of the work. Alwar Balasubramaniam's Drift and Not Just for Us use Tamil Nadu soil to capture nature's marks and patterns. Photograph: ( Indian Pavillion ) While the artwork was being created, peacocks, monkeys and snakes passed through the work in progress, leaving their marks on it. It is a reminder of the idea behind his work: the earth is home to every living creature. Five artists, one idea of home India returned to the Venice Biennale after seven years with an exhibition built around materials familiar to millions of Indians: bamboo, thread, cotton, paper and earth. Through their creations, the five artists brought stories of Partition, traditional architecture, family memories, craftsmanship and India's changing landscapes to an international audience. The exhibition celebrated India's diverse artistic traditions, bringing stories of memory, nature and heritage to a global audience. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) With around 4.5 lakh visitors and an award decided by the public, their exhibition showed how stories rooted in everyday Indian life could resonate with people across the world. Sources: India in Venice 'An Indian postcard from Venice: Why a pavilion at 'Olympics of the art world' matters' by Trisha Mukherjee & Divya A for The Indian Express, Published on 23 September 2026. 'India wins the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the 61st Venice Art Biennale' by Press Information Bureau

Ωστόσο, μια νέα μελέτη προειδοποιεί ότι η αντιμετώπιση της μοναξιάς ως ιατρικής κατάστασης θα μπορούσε να αποσπάσει την προσοχή από τις βαθύτερες κοινωνικές αιτίες της. Ενώ οι επαγγελματίες υγείας μπορούν να προσφέρουν υποστήριξη, οι μόνιμες λύσεις μπορεί να απαιτούν την ανοικοδόμηση των κοινοτήτων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
