items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/science/carbon-dioxide-is-a-climate-problem-it-might-also-be-a-laundry-solution/ . Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Nor did they find a link to seasonal temperature extremes. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity. Ostfeld, et. al. “ The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis .” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Aug. 17, 2026. Image:© Theclarkester | Dreamstime.com

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. The post What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Έφυγε από το συνεδριακό τραπέζι στα δεκατέσσερα
items.titleOriginal: She Left the Conference Table at Fourteen
items.description: Στα δεκατέσσερά της, η Shakhzoda Saidova ξέφυγε από ένα τραπέζι συνεδριάσεων με τη Γενική Συνέλευση του ΟΗΕ και τη UNICEF στο Τατζικιστάν — πολύ νευρική, πολύ πεπεισμένη ότι δεν ανήκε. Αυτό που την έφερε πίσω ήταν μια φράση από έναν μέντορα: μείνετε πιστή σε αυτό που πραγματικά ακούτε από μέσα. Αυτή η γραμμή την ακολουθεί σε κάθε δωμάτιο από τότε. Μεγάλωσε σε ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.

items.title: Η Lily Pad Pic κερδίζει το βραβείο Nature Photographer of the Year, μια «Σπάνια» Τιμή για την εικονογράφηση φυτών

Με τίτλο «The One That Left and The One That Stayed», η φωτογραφία του Hannu Ahonen με ένα φύλλο νούφαρου δίπλα σε ένα παγωμένο αντίγραφο με εικόνα καθρέφτη είναι εκπληκτική στο i…
items.descriptionOriginal: This year’s Nature Photographer of the Year competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in more than 96 countries — and the overall winner, announced Nov. 14, stands out in more ways than one. Titled “The One That Left and the One That Stayed,” Hannu Ahonen’s shot of a water lily leaf beside a mirror-image frozen replica is stunning in its own right, but it’s also a “rare” example of a plant photo winning the annual contest, according to the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom. “It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” Bosboom said in a press release shared with Nice News. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.” He continued, “It takes a moment for the viewer to realize what has happened here: A thin layer of ice that had formed on the leaf has been blown away by the wind. The shapes in the sheet of ice are delicate; even the veins of the water lily leaf are clearly recognizable. Because the water lily and the sheet of ice are still touching, a sense of connection emerges; you realize that they belong together, like yin and yang.” In addition to being named overall winner, the Finnish photographer took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category. Scroll on to see the other category winners and read commentary from the judging panel on each one. Birds: “Painting From the End of the World” by Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel (France) Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel / NPOTY 2026 “Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing. Diagonal lines formed by several trees guide the eyes to discover the bird — expertly framed against the backdrop and placed off-center — while encouraging exploration of the forest and the Patagonian landscape beyond it. Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Mammals: “Play Misty” by Paul Goldstein (U.K.) Paul Goldstein / NPOTY 2026 “Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved. The soft pastel colors create a soothing atmosphere, while the image’s simplicity and quiet emotion ultimately made it stand out among the category’s strongest contenders.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Other Animals: “The Pitcher’s Micro Kingdom” by Marcus Kuan (Singapore) Marcus Kuan / NPOTY 2026 “The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths. As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants? The image invites us to imagine the separate lives of these organisms, briefly brought together. The carefully balanced composition, beautifully controlled lighting, and rich greens and reds against the dark nighttime background make this a striking photograph.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Landscape: “In the Circle of Vultures Around the Falls” by J Fritz Rumpf (U.S.) J Fritz Rumpf / NPOTY 2026 “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left. The interplay of light and shadow transforms the immense power of the waterfalls into something intimate and almost dreamlike. A beautiful example of how an iconic natural wonder can be captured in a truly extraordinary way.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Underwater: “Beneath Aquatic Constellations” by Matt Pérez (U.S.) Matt Pérez / NPOTY 2026 “Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing. Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.The scene feels almost otherworldly, busy with intricate details yet still peaceful to look at — an impressive balance to capture in a single photograph. Its beautiful composition, striking lighting, and balance of rich detail and serene feel made this photo stand out to the jury. Matt Pérez also deserves credit for stepping back from the turtles’ courtship behavior to capture this wider view of a male pond turtle within an extraordinary habitat.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Nature Art: “Peach Blossoms in the Snow” by Xuzhong Liu (China) Xuzhong Liu / NPOTY 2026 “This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colors, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph? The image was taken in September in a wetland area in China, but it reminded the photographer himself of peach blossoms he had previously photographed during a spring trip to Tibet. A good abstract photograph like this also leaves plenty of room for the viewer to decide for themselves what they see in it. This makes it the perfect winner of the nature art category.” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Human and Nature: “Evolution” by Petr Bambousek (Czechia) Petr Bambousek / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife. The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments. The image is both unexpected and unsettling, capturing a broader story of how wildlife is forced to adapt as its natural surroundings are altered and destroyed.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Black and White: “Storm on the Sea” by László Tóth (Hungary) László Tóth / NPOTY 2026 “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer. The black-and-white contrast, dark diagonal lines, and striking patterns create a fascinating abstract composition. It looks like a storm at sea, but in reality, it is a thin layer of snow shaped by strong winds on a frozen lake, captured from above.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Animal Portraits: “A Seal’s Worst Nightmare” by Audun Rikardsen (Norway) Audun Rikardsen / NPOTY 2026 “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear. Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how. Showing something never seen before is a pretty effective method of captivating an audience, and one that carried this image all the way to the top. With oceans warming and ice melting, the ‘What’s going on down there?’ look gives the image a deeper layer of meaning that I appreciate. Right now humanity is looking back up at the bear and shrugging its collective shoulders in pretense. For how much longer?” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Nature of “De Lage Landen”: “Fairies” by Enikő Kálovics (Hungary) Enikő Kálovics / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected. The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.’ The thoughtful use of double exposure adds another layer to the image, capturing not just the insects themselves, but also the sense of wonder and atmosphere of their natural habitat.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Fred Hazelhoff Award, Portfolio: “Eagle Owls in the City” by Simone Baumeister (Germany) Simone Baumeister / NPOTY 2026 “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city. It is clear that she has put a great deal of time into creating the series: She has managed to capture all sorts of special moments with her camera, and the series showcases a wide range of situations, locations, and atmospheres. In doing so, she offers a unique glimpse into the world of a bird that is making a comeback in Germany and which, despite its size, often goes unnoticed by the people around it. Or, as the photographer herself puts it, her images make the invisible visible. And that is one of the great strengths of (nature) photography!” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Youth Photographer of the Year: “Tree of Life” by Parham Pourahmad (U.S.) Parham Pourahmad / NPOTY 2026 “In ‘Tree of Life,’ Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories. Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life. The image combines a beautiful portrait of the animal’s habitat with an intimate glimpse of its hunting behavior.” – Jury member Louis Guillot

items.description: Τις τελευταίες δύο δεκαετίες, πολλές εταιρείες έχουν μειώσει το βάρος των πλαστικών μπουκαλιών, των χαρτοκιβωτίων, των χάρτινων φακέλων και άλλων υλικών συσκευασίας, μια στρατηγική γνωστή ως ελαφρύ βάρος. items.descriptionOriginal: In the last couple of decades, many companies have reduced the heft of plastic bottles , cardboard boxes, paper envelopes, and other packaging materials, a strategy known as lightweighting. At first glance, this seems like a win-win: less material means lower costs and a lighter burden on the environment. But the approach may also backfire, a new study suggests. Researchers found that people are more likely to throw lightweight packaging away, and less likely to recycle it, compared to more substantial packaging materials. “Even well-intended sustainability practices can have unexpected negative consequences,” the researchers write. First, the researchers set out to determine the scope of the problem. A small pilot study at a university campus event and a larger week-long audit of trash and recycling bins on campus showed that lighter-weight recyclable plastic beverage containers were more likely to end up in the trash compared to more substantial plastic cups and bottles. “Once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging,” the researchers write. Investigating causal relationships, the researchers concocted a laboratory study in which participants were asked to assess the properties of a piece of paper—either flimsy newsprint or sturdy cardstock—which they were instructed to dispose of at the end of the experiment. As expected, participants rated the thinner paper as lower quality than the thicker paper and were more likely to throw it in the trash at the end of the experiment—although a statistical analysis people get from recycling has a downside More details about the nuances of people’s thought processes emerged from an online experiment in which participants imagined receiving a takeout meal in either a thin paper bakery bag or a thick paper grocery bag. “Where would you put this bag?” they were asked. The participants then rated the quality of the bag, assessed its value, and indicated their level of discomfort about putting the bag in the garbage. “Ultimately, we find that consumers are more apt to throw low-density packaging in the trash because it is perceived as being more disposable (i.e., lower in value and associated with lesser feelings of waste aversion),” the researchers write. So far, so hopeless, given the human foibles and imperfect decision-making. But the solution could be a relatively simple one, according to the new work. In both an online study and a small field trial, the researchers found evidence that including a message on lightweight packaging—for example, “You may be done with this envelope, but it still has value”—increased the likelihood that the material would make it to the recycling bin. “Prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness,” the researchers write. Issuing such prompts is in companies’ own best interests, the researchers point out. In addition to lightweighting, many firms aim to increase the proportion of recycled material in their packaging. And where is that recycled material going to come from if consumers have thrown the previous iteration of that packaging in the trash? Source: Loomer L. and S.C. Whitley . “ Through thick and thin? When sustainable package design increases consumer waste generation .” Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 2026. Image: © Anthropocene Magazine.

items.title: Ο πωλητής μαθαίνει την ιστορία πίσω από ένα ρυμουλκούμενο και παίρνει μια απόφαση που φέρνει μια οικογένεια σε δάκρυα
items.titleOriginal: Seller Learns the Story Behind a Tow Truck and Makes a Decision That Brings a Family to Tears
items.description: Ένας άντρας από το Μίτσιγκαν που δεν είχε την οικονομική δυνατότητα να αγοράσει πίσω το αγαπημένο ρυμουλκούμενο του παππού του, σκέφτηκε ότι είχε χάσει για πάντα την ευκαιρία του. Αλλά ο άντρας που το πουλούσε είχε άλλα σχέδια, και αυτό που έκανε στη συνέχεια έκανε μια οικογένεια σε κλάματα.
items.descriptionOriginal: A Michigan man who couldn't afford to buy back his late grandfather's beloved tow truck thought he had lost his chance forever. But the man selling it had other plans, and what he did next brought a family to tears.

items.description: Τι μπορεί να είναι σαν να είσαι πουλί; Αρχικά η Helen Lawy πίστευε ότι το να είσαι κιρκινέζι θα σήμαινε ελευθερία. «Λατρεύω τα πουλιά, και ιδιαίτερα τα κικινέζια - όταν αιωρούνται, έχουν μια εκπληκτική εικόνα του τοπίου», λέει. items.descriptionOriginal: W hat might it be like to be a bird? Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles. “Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide — which grew out of the More Than Human Lens Toolkit , developed by anthropologist Patricia Fraga Pérez and philosopher Miguel Prado Casanova — asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough grassland in which to hunt voles and mice, and space undisturbed by people and dogs. Suddenly the landscape around Lawy looked more like a series of obstacles and threats a wild animal needed to conquer: “Once I really began to delve into what it might be like to be a kestrel, I realized actually my options were very limited because it’s so difficult to find areas where I can find food.” Clatworthy dam impounds the headwaters of the River Tone. © River Tone Lawy’s experience is part of a pioneering experiment by Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA), an independent nonprofit initiative hosted by the United Nations Foundation in collaboration with the University of the West of England (UWE) and funded by the Ecological Citizen(s) Network . The project, Risks Beyond Human Eyes, asks people around the River Tone catchment to explore risks not from the conventional perspective of human visitors, landowners, planners or conservationists, but through the sensory worlds and needs of other species: fierce otter, threatened salmon, quiet red deer, sharp-sighted kestrel or blind earthworm. Over a period of several months, 18 participants swam like salmon, surfed the river to mimic how an otter might glide through the water, or hid in hollows like earthworms. The setup sounds fanciful until its practical implications emerge: If conventional risk assessments systematically overlook what matters to other species, could temporarily shifting the human viewpoint reveal problems — and solutions — that would otherwise remain invisible? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] For Lawy, it has already changed how she manages land. She came to the project as a local resident, concerned about the water quality of the River Tone. People want to bathe in it, yet the water is too polluted with runoff from the nearby fields, herbicides, pesticides and other toxins. “But animals haven’t got that choice,” she says. “They are constantly living in this very poor-quality water.” These insights are part of the logic of the ASRA project, challenging the human-centeredness of conventional risk assessment. “Of course we’re not pretending that a person literally becomes an otter or kestrel,” project co-director Phil Tovey explains, “but this kind of disciplined attention exposes aspects of an animal’s environment that humans routinely fail to notice.” The resulting testimonies are not intended simply to produce moving stories about wildlife, but are treated as input to a wider systemic-risk assessment, alongside scientific and other evidence such as water quality. Participants in the project working on a course of action. Credit: Darren Honeywell According to the 2026 Living Planet Index , freshwater species populations declined by 85 percent between 1970 and 2022 , the steepest decline of any of the major ecosystems assessed. It’s one thing to read this number as an intellectual piece of information and another to attempt the perspective of a salmon, like some of the study participants, and arrive at the life-threatening realization that they couldn’t overcome a river barrier to get to their food source. Lawy experienced firsthand that a landscape designed to look accessible and attractive to humans appears radically different to a species trying to feed and reproduce. While repeatedly sitting outside over several weeks, Lawy never actually saw a kestrel. There were too many people, too many dogs, too much disturbance. “Kestrels actually need some space from us,” she realized. Lawy also saw the hay meadows in a different light. Once the hay is cut, Lawy suddenly noticed, the landscape can become a stark, hostile expanse. “There is no cover,” she says. During a hot, dry summer, that lack of shelter can mean the difference between life and death. At the next meeting of Friends of Longrun Meadow, Lawy proposed a “mosaic of habitats,” retaining more long grass and larger riparian margins alongside the river instead of the more manicured grounds. The River Tone under the M5. © River Tone Lawy says she now asks people to adopt a new perspective. “I want you to think more from an animal perspective,” she tells them. “Rather than us thinking we need to trim that hedge, are we leaving places for birds and insects and all these other species who live here? Are we providing feeding corridors for bats?” Much to her surprise, the group “straightforwardly accepted these insights,” Lawy reports. The larger ambition of ASRA’s experiment is to translate these observations into protective action. Phil Tovey, who co-leads the project with Miguel Prado Casanova of UWE, describes the River Tone as a system in which risks compound. For instance, research has found that kestrels living within 30 meters of a major road show elevated cortisol from stress, and they shift from reproduction towards survival. “So when we then look at overall coverage of roads in the region, you can just see the scale of harm, disruption, physical and mental injury that is really widespread,” Tovey concludes. “One of the things that we do in ASRA for a systemic risk response is we look at the underlying structures, the historical conditions and what are the barriers to transformation.” A former Royal Marines Commando, Tovey served on operations across the world, from peacekeeping in Northern Ireland to working with indigenous forces in Afghanistan and deployments across Africa and the Middle East. Before joining ASRA, he worked as the Head of Futures in the U.K.’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Rain patters downstream of French Weir. © River Tone He likens the emotional testimonies of the study participants to the shocked reports of civilians caught in war zones. He also conducted roughly two dozen of his own field experiments, switching between species and testing the instructions given to participants. “I’d be going out at four in the morning, roughly knowing where the red deer hang out.” For Tovey, connecting the participants’ testimonies to scientific evidence and a structured framework for mapping risk means “setting the conditions for deeper structural change.” For example, the river and its tributaries contain more than 337 weirs and other obstacles over about 33 kilometers, creating problems for migrating salmon and other creatures. “No one has really considered the density and volume of these pressures on the animals,” Tovey says. “But when I sit as an otter, I see these barriers because as an otter I’m only about six centimeters off the ground.” Conventional assessments tend to divide problems into categories: transport, agriculture, water quality, habitat, biodiversity. Tovey’s digital mapping of the River Tone risks is effectively “bright orange” as different risks overlap. The problem is not merely the number of individual hazards, but their density and interaction. Changing the perspective does not mean abandoning scientific evidence, but it can show which actions will have the most impact. “As a research team, asking a bunch of humans to try and inevitably fail to engage in living as a chosen animal, the absurdity of trying to actually do that was taken really seriously,” says Tovey, addressing the obvious criticism of anthropomorphism. “We never once claimed that Helen was a kestrel, but using the structured process we set out, we need to make an imaginary leap to calibrate what that environment would be like for the animal. Then we start to see barriers in a different way.” The research team briefing the Systemic Risk Assessment. Credit: Darren Honeywell For Lawy, the exercise in changing perspective led to changes in land management, and then to a recognition that she wants to press for changes beyond her local group. “It’s amazing how quickly that local action on a relatively small area can lead you to realize that actually we need some policy changes within the landscape to really make that difference,” she says. The project inspired an even more ambitious question: What does the river need? One of the study participants works in the city council. According to Tovey, “she became instrumental in stitching together the work and applying it to River Tone as a subjective person.” A working group quickly formed, resulting in the adaptation of Somerset’s very first River Rights Charter, which recognizes the river’s rights to regenerate, flow and be protected from harm. Lawy’s stint as a kestrel is part of a growing global movement to shift from an anthropocentric view, inspired by programs such as NYU Law School’s More than Human Life as well as bestselling authors like Charles Foster , whose book Being A Beast portrayed him living as badger, deer, fox and swift. It also marks a return to Indigenous values. In 2008, Indigenous peoples led Ecuador to become the world’s first country to formally recognize the “Rights of Mother Earth,” a ruling that the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature (GARN) and others subsequently used successfully against a road construction company that dumped rubble into the Vilcabamba River. As a result, the government was forced to clean up the river. Tovey agrees that rivers and other elements of nature should have the right to be represented. “I have never met my MP,” he says. “Yet we accept political representation for humans. What’s problematic is making sure it’s done with integrity.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The approach remains experimental. There are obvious limits to humans attempting to understand other species, and the researchers themselves acknowledge the need for more time. But Tovey hopes to expand ASRA’s work to larger areas. “We have started to forge connections with our sister rivers, reaching out to those groups and thinking about a wider solidarity movement,” Tovey says, intending to integrate the lessons from the River Tone project. Lawy’s experience suggests another potential benefit: changing what people care about. “One of the really important things that’s come out of this for me,” she says, “is the emotional connection that you get back with nature.” That emotional connection is not taken as a substitute for evidence. Rather, it can make evidence harder to ignore. The post The People Who Became Wildlife appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: The bots roll along blood vessels to stir up stagnant blood and push drugs toward clots. Drugs that break up blood clots are vital for treating strokes, heart attacks, and clogged blood vessels in the lungs, but sometimes blockages are so large that medication struggles to get through. Now, researchers are building tiny magnetic robots to help medicines reach their targets. Severe blockages in blood vessels pose a tricky problem. The bloodstream is the only way to deliver clot-busting drugs, but if a clot stops the flow, there is no other way to carry them there. A team at ETH Zurich in Switzerland has a workaround. Magnetically driven microbots that roll along vessel walls can stir up stagnant blood so the drug gets pushed towards the clot. In lab tests, the approach dissolved clots six times faster than with the drug alone, and in experiments on pigs, it restored blood flow to an area twice as large after 30 minutes. “To our knowledge, we are the first to show in a clinically relevant large-animal model that the use of microrobots in this way does indeed enhance thrombolysis [the process of dissolving blood clots],” Schürle said in a press release . The bots are a far cry from your traditional robot. Just eight micrometers long, each is shaped like a grain of rice and made of a sugar-based polymer laced with magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. During fabrication, the researchers expose the devices to a rotating magnetic field that pushes the nanoparticles into a straight line, essentially creating a bar magnet running the length of each bot. When a magnetic control system outside the body applies a rotating field, the internal magnet spins and causes each bot to tumble head over tail. The bots themselves don’t carry drugs. Rather, they’re released near a blockage along with clot-busting medicine. As the bots roll along the vessel walls towards the restriction, they create currents that carry the drug into the clot. To test the approach, the team built an artificial network of vessel-like channels and plugged it with clots made of pig blood. They compared what happened when they added the clot-dissolving drug alone to what happened when they added the drug and the bots together. Adding the bots cleared the clots six times faster than when they tried just the drug. To see if the strategy would work in real biological systems, the team blocked arteries in live pigs and treated them with just drugs and drugs plus microbots. After 30 minutes, the area with restored blood flow was twice as large in animals that received the bots. The work adds to a growing body of research into clot-busting magnetic microrobots. Last year, a separate ETH Zurich team led by Bradley Nelson published a paper in Science describing a dissolvable gel capsule that could be steered through blood vessels and release a clot-dissolving drug when heated by a high-frequency magnetic field. Others have taken a more mechanical approach. Researchers at the University of Twente and Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands used 3D-printed, screw-shaped robots containing tiny magnets to drill into clots, removing enough material from a blocked artery taken from a sheep to get blood flowing again. While the ETH team have filed a patent application for their bots, it’s still early. The paper describing the results has yet to clear peer review, and human trials are a long way off. Nonetheless, the results are another indication that microrobots could one day become a valuable new tool in a doctor’s arsenal. items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says.
